other-interests-84518c5d65.fulltext:
The data center boom was on Tuesday ballots 41 times. It won once
Across 10 states this Election Day, voters overwhelmingly backed restrictions on data center development or rejected measures that would have eased their construction
On Tuesday the artificial intelligence boom was on the ballot 41 times in 10 states. By Wednesday, with most results in, voters had sided with it just once.
The questions, many of them in Ohio, spanned moratoriums, attempted rezonings and advisory votes for local officials. Another six preceded them this year; a further three are yet to come. In many cases, the margins were staggering. In Wells, Me., more than 80 percent of voters approved a retroactive 180-day moratorium on data center development.

india-26e037c469.headline: Trump's midterm setback may give India an edge in trade deal
india-26e037c469.fulltext:
New Delhi: The US has sought to allay concerns that the Republicans’ midterm election defeat could derail trade talks with India, with an American embassy spokesperson telling Mint that President Donald Trump remains firmly in charge of Washington’s trade agenda.
Experts in India see challenges as well as opportunity from the development. While a Democrat-controlled Congress could make the ratification of a trade deal harder to accomplish, Trump’s political setback may also give New Delhi greater leverage at the negotiating table.
President Trump “remains firmly in command” of the country's foreign policy, including the trade agenda, the embassy spokesperson in New Delhi, said. “The midterm election results do not change our commitment to strengthening our partnership (with India),” the spokesperson said in response to Mint’s query on whether the Democratic control of the Congress would in any way impact the ongoing trade deal negotiations.
American voters have given the opposition Democratic Party control of the US Congress and flipped key gubernatorial posts. Trump’s Republican Party faced stunning defeats in its strongholds such as Texas, Georgia, Iowa and Ohio, where it lost the governors’ posts to the Democrats.
Indian strategic and trade experts reckoned that the setback to Trump's party could bring in fresh uncertainty over the trade deal prospects. Any agreement on the trade deal will need the Congress backing to be ratified, complicating the path to a final deal, they said.
“I think it would be very difficult for Trump to give us substantial comparative advantage in the trade deal vis-a-vis our competitors, as there is uncertainty now over Congress’ backing to any such deal,” said Jayant Dasgupta, former Indian Ambassador to the World Trade Organization.
But the result also opens a window to repair ties strained in recent years over India's purchases of Russian oil, with New Delhi asserting it will take all necessary steps to ensure its energy security amid geopolitical conflicts that have disrupted supplies and pushed up oil prices.
A White House facing fresh political constraints may now be more willing to accommodate India’s concerns, while New Delhi could enter any fresh rounds of talks with a stronger leverage, experts said.
“India now has greater leverage, and I hope we use it well,” said Biswajit Dhar, economist and a former professor at the Jawaharlal Nehru University.
Commerce and industry minister Piyush Goyal had last month exuded optimism about an early closure and operationalization of the trade agreement, but only after India secures an export advantage over its competitors.
The US is India’s largest export market. India’s exports to the US were at $87 billion last fiscal.
Queries on the impact of the US midterm election result on India emailed to the spokespersons for the ministries of finance and external affairs did not receive an immediate response. A spokesperson for the commerce and industry ministry declined to comment.
Energy and markets
The poll outcome could calm the global oil markets if Trump steps back from escalating the ongoing war in West Asia, the experts said. But some flagged near-term risk of escalation in tensions in West Asia before the new Congress convenes in January.
Trump’s tariff strategy and war policies may face increased US Congress scrutiny in the coming months, which may result in unintended uncertainties in terms of trade policies towards India and investment flows, they said.
Brent futures were down 8.9% to $94.29 a barrel at 10.45 PM, the lowest level since 4 September, as Trump played down the prospect of Iran strikes following the Democratic sweep. Stocks of AI companies tumbled, as investors braced for greater regulation.
The Indian rupee stayed firm for the second straight session to settle 29 paise higher at 94.46 against the dollar, supported by easing crude oil prices. As of 10.45 pm pm India time, the Dow Jones Industrial Average was up 2.9%, while the Nasdaq composite was up 2.1% higher. The Gift Nifty traded up 1.75%, indicating a strong opening for the local market.
Some policy experts advised a wait-and-watch policy for India. “We have to wait to assess how Trump may react post midterm defeat, as given his personality, he may become more reactive towards India and internationally to distract domestic public attention,” said Ram Singh, an international trade expert and a professor at IIFT, New Delhi.
Energy experts expect some measure of stability in the global oil market. Manas Majumdar, leader, oil and gas at PwC noted that the results may restrict a further escalation in the war with Iran, thereby easing oil prices.
"This will put a curb on Trump. Although it may not result in an immediate policy change, it may lead to a faster closure to the war against Iran, which will ease the prices of oil," Majumdar said.
The Democrats have been largely against Trump's tariff regime, so some relief on that front is expected, said Prashant Vashisht, senior vice-president and co-group head, corporate ratings, at Icra Ratings.

indian-startups-1bd72439b4.headline: Razorpay Gets SEBI Nod For ₹6,000 Cr IPO
indian-startups-1bd72439b4.fulltext: Fintech major Razorpay has received SEBI’s approval for its proposed ₹5,000-6,000 Cr IPO, sources told Inc42. The offering is expected to value the company at around $5 Bn, with a listing likely between January and March 2027, the sources added. The IPO is expected to comprise a fresh issue and an offer-for-sale (OFS). However, the proposed split could not be ascertained. The Economic Times first reported the development. Founded in 2014 by Shashank Kumar and Harshil Mathur, Razorpay offers payment processing, business banking, payroll, and lending solutions. It filed its IPO papers through the confidential route in June, targeting a valuation of $5 Bn to $6 Bn, below the $7.5 Bn valuation it commanded in its last funding round in 2021. Ahead of the listing, Razorpay shifted its domicile from the US to India. The company slipped into the red in FY25, weighed down by ₹1,209 Cr in ESOP expenses and one-time restructuring and tax costs linked to the move. Operating revenue rose 65% to ₹3,783 Cr during the year. Razorpay’s Growing AI Offerings Alongside its IPO preparations, Razorpay has been expanding its AI offerings across payments, marketing, and business operations. Last month, it announced an expanded partnership with OpenAI to help Indian brands advertise on ChatGPT. Under the partnership, its growth marketing platform, Razorpay Engage, will enable brands to prepare product catalogues and launch and manage campaigns on ChatGPT Ads. Razorpay has also launched Vulcan, a transformer-based AI foundation model for digital payments. The company claims the model can improve payment reliability and safety by scoring payment routes in real time and identifying fraud patterns across multiple merchants once deployed. Built using NVIDIA and AWS technology, Vulcan combines Razorpay’s payments data with NVIDIA’s accelerated computing and AWS’ cloud infrastructure. The fintech major has also been developing Agent Studio, a platform for deploying task-specific AI agents for businesses. Around 200 businesses were using the platform in beta as of August, with use cases spanning reconciliation, abandoned-cart recovery, subscription recovery, and finance operations. Razorpay has raised over $800 Mn to date from investors including Y Combinator, Tiger Global Management, Ribbit Capital, and Lightspeed.

work-careers-5e56872780.headline: India's FDE hiring boom exposes a training dilemma for IT firms
work-careers-5e56872780.fulltext:

The emerging talent gap assumes significance as Indian IT companies increasingly reorganise delivery teams around AI agents and smaller groups of engineers responsible for business outcomes.
  November 04, 2026 / 15:30 IST  
Indian IT services companies are stepping up efforts to build a workforce of forward-deployed engineers (FDEs) as artificial intelligence (AI) changes how technology projects are delivered. However, the push is exposing a talent dilemma i.e., companies need engineers who can independently deploy AI solutions at customer organisations, but developing those capabilities requires experience that cannot be acquired through conventional classroom training alone.
The challenge is forcing IT firms to adopt a two-pronged approach, combining external recruitment with internal upskilling, even as demand for engineers with a mix of technical expertise, business understanding and client-facing skills continues to outstrip availability.
Forward-deployed engineers work directly with customers to identify business problems, develop AI-powered solutions and take them into production. Unlike traditional software engineering roles, which often separate development, consulting and client engagement, FDEs are expected to take responsibility for the entire deployment process.
The emerging talent gap assumes significance as Indian IT companies increasingly reorganise delivery teams around AI agents and smaller groups of engineers responsible for business outcomes, rather than relying solely on large teams executing predefined tasks.
According to a report by Scaler and CyberMedia Research (CMR), 88 percent of surveyed enterprises expect demand for FDE capabilities to increase by 2030, while only 1 percent of engineers currently hold explicit FDE roles.
IT firms turn to internal talent
HCLTech is among the large IT services companies attempting to build FDE capabilities by training engineers recruited from campuses.
During the September quarter of FY27, the company onboarded 6,136 freshers, of whom approximately 15 percent were recruited under its elite engineer category. These employees are expected to undergo further training to become forward-deployed engineers.
HCLTech is also launching an enterprise-wide FDE Academy, with training tracks aligned to technologies from OpenAI, Anthropic, Amazon Web Services, Google and Nvidia, alongside a programme being developed with Microsoft.
However, the company acknowledged that freshly recruited engineers cannot be expected to immediately perform the responsibilities of an FDE.
LTM is adopting a similar approach, combining recruitment with the retraining of existing employees.
"We are hiring FDs, but at the same time we are training our own people also to become FDs," LTM chief executive officer Venu Lambu told Moneycontrol.
Lambu said the company was looking to accelerate hiring in data and AI-related areas while upgrading the capabilities of its existing workforce.
Amar Srivastava, CEO of Online Business and Group CPO at Scaler, said companies are increasingly looking to develop FDE talent internally but are struggling to find employees who possess the full range of skills required.
"I think the long-term strategy is 60 to 70% of the talent that is in-house if it can be upskilled," Srivastava told Moneycontrol, describing the approach being considered by companies.
A separate September 2026 white paper by Futurense's FDE Academy highlights the imbalance between engineering capabilities and the broader requirements of enterprise AI deployment.
It also found that 70 percent of FDE-type professionals have eight years of experience or less, while just 6 percent have more than 15 years of experience.
A new delivery model takes shape
Wipro is also building FDE capabilities as part of its transition towards AI-native delivery.
The company's AI-native business unit has more than 2,000 engineers, including FDEs, and is working on engagements involving AI-enabled platforms and outcome-based contracts.
Wipro chief executive officer Srinivas Pallia said the company was developing FDE capabilities both within its AI-native unit and through technology partnerships, with engineers expected to combine technical expertise and domain understanding.
Meanwhile, Coforge is moving towards hybrid human-agent delivery teams supported by FDEs.
Chief executive officer Sudhir Singh said the company sees hybrid teams of engineers and AI agents as an important part of its future delivery model, as it moves from AI-assisted engineering towards AI-led execution.

deep-tech-b93ebfd1ec.headline: Agility Robotics is taking humanoid robots public in a first for Wall Street
deep-tech-b93ebfd1ec.fulltext:
Agility Robotics is about to give Wall Street a reality check on the humanoid robot boom.
The Oregon startup, whose two-legged robots carry heavy materials and sort goods in factories and warehouses, is expected to begin trading on Nasdaq on Thursday, becoming the first humanoid-focused company to go public in the US. Its financial disclosures show just how far the industry still has to go before robots become a profitable business.
Agility brought in just $1.8 million in revenue last year while reporting a $138.1 million net loss, according to its merger filings. More than half its revenue came from five robots purchased by one of its investors.
Agility is going public through a merger with Churchill Capital Corp XI, a special-purpose acquisition company (SPAC) led by former Citigroup executive Michael Klein, which was completed Wednesday. The combined company is expected to begin trading under the ticker AGLT when the market opens Thursday.
"There's something to be said for being first," Agility CEO Peggy Johnson, who previously led Magic Leap and held roles at Microsoft and Qualcomm, told Business Insider. "We will be able to set many of the metrics, if you will, on what customers need in a humanoid."
The merger valued Agility's existing equity at about $2.5 billion. The company expects about $465 million in gross capital before expenses, including $100 million already received.
SPAC mergers boomed in 2020 and 2021, before collapsing as interest rates rose in 2022. They are drawing renewed interest as the IPO market recovers. Johnson said Agility chose the route to bring in Klein, a prolific SPAC sponsor known for helping take Sam Altman-backed nuclear power company Oklo and electric vehicle maker Lucid public.
"Agility is unique to the industry because they're actually deployed," George Chowdhury, a principal analyst at ABI Research, told Business Insider. "In the grand scheme of things, the deployments are very small, but it's big for commercial humanoids."
Agility has deployed Digit, its humanoid robot, across nine customer facilities, including those belonging to Amazon, Toyota, and the logistics company GXO. Its investors include Amazon, Foxconn, Nvidia, SoftBank, and Silicon Valley venture firm DCVC.
Agility's losses aren't just on paper. While about $38 million of the company's $138.1 million net loss came from non-cash expenses tied to employee stock awards, filings show that the company used $99.8 million in cash to run the business in 2025. Agility lost $2.7 million on its sales, even before research and other company expenses.
"We expect to incur additional losses and higher operating expenses for the foreseeable future," the company said in SEC filings.
"There's a lot of challenges when it comes to solving unit economics," Michelle Sun, a robotics analyst who writes the Substack Core Matter, told Business Insider.
Agility is betting on Digit 5, its newest robot, to grow its business. Digit 5 is designed to safely work near people without the safety barriers required by earlier versions.
The company's filing says it has more than $300 million in orders for 1,000 robots from a single customer. This customer would pay to use the robots over a three-year period. But those orders depend on Agility meeting deadlines and delivering robots with the promised features.
Agility is targeting deliveries in the first half of 2027 and general availability by the end of that year.
The company's public debut highlights a striking divide in how investors value humanoid robotics companies.
Agility's $2.5 billion valuation is well below those of some privately held humanoid rivals, including Bay Area-based Figure AI at about $39 billion, Texas-based Apptronik at about $5.5 billion, and Germany-based Neura Robotics at around $7 billion. Tesla is also developing its own humanoid, Optimus, but the project doesn't have a standalone valuation.
"This is a trend we're seeing, where companies with deployments who are actually shipping hardware today are valued by the market a lot lower than companies that are betting on this future," Chowdhury said.
Sun said that Agility's listing would provide a reference point for how public markets value a company that makes humanoids, a form factor that remains controversial among both experts and investors.
Agility's public listing comes as Washington tightens restrictions on foreign-made robots, potentially giving US manufacturers an edge. In July, the Federal Communications Commission banned new foreign-made "advanced robotic devices," including humanoids, quadrupeds, and some robot vacuums. Agility manufactures Digit at its Oregon factory.
The humanoid market is currently dominated by Chinese companies such as Unitree, which went public on the Shanghai stock exchange this summer and has a market value of around $40 billion. Chinese robotics firms accounted for about 90% of humanoid robot shipments last year, according to Omdia.
"It's good for the US to show strength in this area," Johnson told Business Insider.

india-143b567222.headline: India approves $297 million incentive policy for lithium, nickel processing
india-143b567222.fulltext:
India’s cabinet approved on Wednesday an incentive policy worth 28.14 billion rupees ($297 million) to boost domestic processing of lithium and nickel, the government said in a statement, in a move aimed at reducing the country’s reliance on supply chains dominated by China.
India has a high import dependence on critical minerals such as lithium, and tighter conditions following export controls by China create potential supply-chain vulnerability, the government had said in March.
On Wednesday, it unveiled a programme seeking to bolster processing of lithium and nickel ores and intermediary products into high purity compounds.
It listed electric mobility, battery energy storage systems, electronics, defence and speciality steel as beneficiaries of the programme.
“Processing of critical minerals remains geographically concentrated in a few global locations. This exposes supply chains to geopolitical disruptions, price volatility, and potential supply restrictions,” the statement said.
This has implications for national security and economic sovereignty, it said.
The programme would push India towards self-reliance and support the development of domestic processing infrastructure, it added.

Fal, an AI inference startup that hosts image, video and audio models for creators and developers, has doubled its valuation to $16 billion in a new round of funding.
Bessemer Venture Partners, an existing investor, led a $1.3 billion financing round in the startup in October, Fal is set to announce Tuesday. Other investors include Nvidia Corp., Sound Ventures, HOF Capital and T. Rowe Price Associates Inc. Fal previously raised $350 million in a Sequoia-led round in April at an $8 billion valuation.
Fal’s business has expanded in response to developers’ growing appetite for more inference, or the process of running AI systems after they’ve been trained. Other startups offering AI inferencing services, including Modal and Baseten, have also been in discussions to raise money at steep valuations, Bloomberg News previously reported.
Fal opted to raise such a large amount in part because a surge of demand meant it needed to get more computing power, said chief executive officer and co-founder Burkay Gur. “We hit a point in summer where we were not able to serve our customers and had to rate limit them,” Gur said.

A KsheerasagarPublished4 Nov 2026, 11:38 PM IST A Democratic sweep of both chambers of Congress in the midterm elections left Wall Street divided in Wednesday's trade. While AI chipmakers, memory companies and data centre operators fell, hyperscalers surged sharply. Shares of Amazon surged 8% to a three-month high, while Apple and Microsoft advanced 6% each. Alphabet gained 5.7%, while Meta Platforms climbed 3.5%, powering a rally on Wall Street after days of selling fuelled by concerns over the soaring costs of the AI boom. Apple, which has avoided Big Tech's massive AI spending but is feeling the impact of an AI-fuelled surge in memory chip prices, jumped nearly 7% to a record high. If the gains hold, the five companies are on course to add more than $750 billion in combined market value, according to Bloomberg. A Democratic-led Congress could push for tighter regulation of AI development and data centre construction. Some investors see this as a sign that hyperscalers may moderate their spending. On the other hand, SanDisk shares slumped 10%, while peer Seagate Technology Holdings plunged 8.2% at its intraday low. Nvidia, the chipmaker that quickly became the poster child of the AI stock frenzy, slipped 2.5%. CoreWeave, a company that rents out access to AI chips to customers over the cloud, fell 11%. Advanced Micro Devices, another chip giant, was down 1.5%, even after reporting a much stronger profit for the latest quarter than analysts had expected. For hyperscalers, the rally marks a sharp reversal after a difficult period for cloud giants. Their quarterly earnings reports highlighted how the race to build AI infrastructure was turning once cash-rich, debt-light companies into heavy spenders increasingly reliant on borrowing. Microsoft was a notable exception, reporting $18.6 billion in cash flow. Democrats have voiced opposition to data centre expansion, including in Texas. The results could accelerate a backlash against the power-hungry, water-intensive and noisy facilities that are central to the AI boom but have become increasingly unpopular with local communities. The tech giants have been building capacity at a blistering pace, with plans to spend more than $740 billion this year, up from roughly $400 billion last year, as per Bloomberg. The artificial intelligence industry has remained volatile for months amid criticism that valuations have risen too far and that the sector could be in a bubble. Concerns are growing that the hundreds of billions of dollars Big Tech companies are pouring into AI data centres may not generate enough productivity gains and profits to justify the investments. The latest earnings reports from Alphabet and other Big Tech companies also highlighted how AI-related investments may be weighing on their existing businesses. Google's parent company reported a larger cash outflow, as measured by free cash flow, during the latest quarter, alongside slower-than-expected growth in its search business. US President Donald Trump has been a strong supporter of the AI industry, and Democratic control of Capitol Hill could bring greater regulation or restrictions for the sector. Concerns about AI have, however, been growing across political parties. State-level policy changes could have a more immediate impact on the industry. Democrats won gubernatorial races in Ohio, Georgia and Texas, three states with significant planned data centre investments. Their incoming governors have pledged greater oversight of the sector. In Ohio, Democratic Senator-elect Sherrod Brown made opposition to data centre expansion a central part of his campaign. ai-6671c4c994.headline: India’s AI regulation consultation paper nearing completion: Report
ai-6671c4c994.fulltext:
Centre’s AI regulation consultation paper nearing completion, public feedback expected soon
The Centre is close to finalising its consultation paper on artificial intelligence (AI) regulation and is expected to invite public feedback on the proposed safeguards, Moneycontrol reported, citing people familiar with the matter.
The government has examined regulatory frameworks adopted internationally and held discussions with several stakeholders, including academics, while preparing the document, a senior government official said.
The consultation is expected to address concerns around AI safety, the spread of deepfakes and the potential psychological impact of the technology on users. It will also examine skilling requirements and ways to ensure that the gains from AI are accessible to a wider section of society.
Union Electronics and Information Technology Minister Ashwini Vaishnaw first announced the proposed consultation on October 8. At the time, he said the government intended to publish the paper within a month, identifying AI safety as a key area of focus.
On October 23, Vaishnaw reiterated that the document would be released in the coming weeks and said the government would invite responses from citizens, businesses and AI users. He also indicated that the scale of emerging AI-related risks warranted consideration of legislative measures and additional regulations.
What the existing AI governance guidelines propose
The exercise builds on the India AI Governance Guidelines released in November 2025. The framework outlined seven guiding principles for the development and deployment of AI, including maintaining human oversight wherever feasible, establishing accountability in proportion to potential harm and ensuring transparency for users and regulators.
The committee responsible for drafting the guidelines observed that several risks associated with AI could be addressed through existing legislation. However, it recommended examining gaps in the legal framework, particularly around accountability when AI systems cause harm, the application of data protection requirements to AI development and copyright issues involving material used to train AI models.
The guidelines also highlighted the need for uniform mechanisms to establish the origin and authenticity of digital content, particularly amid growing concerns over deepfakes.
On the institutional front, the framework proposed setting up an AI Governance Group to coordinate policymaking across government departments, backed by a Technology and Policy Expert Committee. It also recommended establishing an AI Safety Institute to facilitate research and testing.

Isomorphic Labs, the artificial intelligence (AI) drug discovery startup spun out of Alphabet Inc (NASDAQ:GOOG)'s Google DeepMind, is in early talks to raise new funding at a valuation of at least $40 billion.
The London-based company could be valued as high as $50 billion in the financing, although the talks are ongoing and terms could change before any deal closes, a report by Bloomberg said.
The potential valuation would represent a sharp increase from just five months ago, when Isomorphic Labs raised $2.1 billion in a Series B funding round that included substantial backing from Alphabet.
Isomorphic Labs was founded in 2021 to build on AlphaFold, DeepMind's AI system for predicting the three-dimensional structures of proteins, a capability that can help researchers understand how potential medicines interact with biological targets.
The startup is competing with technology companies and biotechnology firms seeking to use AI to reduce the time and cost of discovering and developing new drugs.
Few AI drug discovery companies have yet progressed treatments into clinical trials, and none has brought an AI-designed medicine to market, highlighting the long development timelines and risks involved.
Chief executive Demis Hassabis, who is also Alphabet's chief scientist and chairman of DeepMind, has said he wants to reduce the time required to develop new medicines from years to months.

Peppermint Robotics, which makes autonomous cleaning robots, has raised Rs 100 crore (about $10.5 million) in a pre-Series B round led by pi Ventures and Crane Venture Partners. Asiana Fund also participated in the round.
The Pune- and Austin-based startup said it doubled its revenue last year and grew nearly sixfold between FY24 and FY26. It last raised Rs 34 crore ($4 million) in a Series A round in April 2025. Peppermint has a presence in nine countries, with the US being its biggest market.
Founded in 2019 at the Society for Innovation and Entrepreneurship at IIT Bombay, the company's autonomous cleaning robots are deployed across a range of commercial and industrial environments, including factories, hospitals, airports, malls, warehouses, hotels and universities. Its machines scrub floors and move materials in factories, hospitals, airports, malls, warehouses, hotels and universities. They are designed to fit into existing routines rather than disrupt workflows.
The company primarily serves facility management companies that oversee cleaning operations, including the selection of equipment, chemicals and cleaning processes.
One of its more challenging deployments is at a global pharmaceutical company, where its cleanroom robots have passed qualification testing in an EU GMP Grade cleanroom, among the most tightly regulated settings a cleaning robot can enter, Peppermint said, in a statement.
Cleanroom robots are specialised manipulators engineered to operate in controlled, contamination-free environments.
The startup builds its hardware, software and perception systems in-house and assembles its robots in Pune. They run on proprietary Peppermint OS, using computer vision and LiDAR to map spaces, plan routes, and avoid obstacles. Operators can monitor them in real time through a cloud dashboard. For security-sensitive sites, the company offers fully offline 'stealth' robots that meet stringent information securtiy requirements.
Runal Dahiwade, Founder and CEO of Peppermint Robotics, said, "Cleaning teams keep hospitals, factories and airports running. Our robots work alongside them and take on the most repetitive, physically demanding jobs, like floor scrubbing and material transportation. Our customers judge us on one thing: a clean floor, every shift.
"So we build our robots heavy-duty, to last multiple years, and we stay with every machine for its whole lifecycle. This round lets us build more of them, closer to our customers worldwide."
The newly raised capital will go towards next-generation robotics and expanding manufacturing capacity. An assembly line in North America is also being planned over the coming months.
Peppermint also intends to step up business development in the United States and Asia, grow its presence in Europe, and hire senior leaders and engineers.
On the product side, it plans to widen its range of floor-cleaning and material-handling robots and develop its cleanroom line.
Shubham Sandeep, Partner at pi Ventures, pointed to the company's "clear ROI" in demanding settings such as healthcare and hospitality. Anandamoy Roychowdhary of Crane Venture Partners said Peppermint has built a production-grade cleanroom robot for mission-critical businesses. Neha Aggarwal of Asiana Fund called the company the kind of advanced manufacturing business India can build for global markets.

global-economics-fddb8470c5.headline: From tunnel boring machines to rockets and pod taxis, L&T explores new manufacturing bets
global-economics-fddb8470c5.fulltext:
MUMBAI: Larsen and Toubro Ltd (L&T) is looking to expand beyond building infrastructure projects and become a bigger manufacturer, exploring at least half a dozen new businesses ranging from nuclear fuel rods and tunnel boring machines to rockets and drones and their components. The move is aimed at diversifying a business still heavily dependent on project execution, as the company approaches ₹3 trillion in annual revenue and seeks to sustain growth of 12-15%.
The Mumbai-based engineering and construction major is also evaluating opportunities in pod taxis, battery energy storage systems (BESS), traction motors for electric vehicles, and prefabricated residential units, including modular bedrooms and bathrooms that can be installed at construction sites to speed up building, company executives said.
These prospective businesses would add to L&T's existing manufacturing portfolio, which spans defence equipment such as howitzers, rocket launchers, warships and the upcoming Zorawar tank, as well as industrial valves, construction equipment and electrolyzers. The manufacturing and products segment accounted for 6% of the company's ₹1.47 trillion revenue in the first half of fiscal year 2027 (FY27), according to the L&T's latest investor presentation.
“Our portfolio is very project overweight,” R. Shankar Raman, L&T’s president and whole-time director for finance, had said during a media interaction on 28 October.
He said technology and financial services have helped reduce the company's dependence on project-led businesses, but the portfolio remained skewed. L&T wants to at least double the contribution of manufacturing to its business, Shankar Raman added.
A spokesperson for L&T confirmed that the company was evaluating opportunities to manufacture drones, battery energy storage systems (BESS), rocket components, tunnel boring machines and electric vehicle (EV) motors. The spokesperson did not comment on whether nuclear fuel rods, pod taxis or complete rockets were also under consideration.
New manufacturing bets
Several opportunities are linked to anticipated policy changes and emerging demand. L&T expects the entry of private players into India's nuclear energy sector under the new nuclear energy law to create a shortage of nuclear fuel rods, which are thin metal tubes packed with small pellets of nuclear fuel. The company sees this as a potential manufacturing opportunity.
It is also considering making rockets for satellite launches as the government opens up the space sector to private participation. The government is reportedly considering transferring Indian Space Research Organisation (Isro) technology to private players for manufacturing.
Pod taxis, small vehicles designed to carry a handful of passengers on dedicated tracks, are another possibility. The Maharashtra government is planning India's first pod taxi system in Mumbai's Bandra Kurla Complex business district. However, the project has been awarded to Hyderabad-based Sai Green Mobility Pvt. Ltd.
L&T is also developing a prototype tunnel boring machine, which it could eventually manufacture at scale for its own projects as well as for sale to other companies.
“If India is going to build more and more networks underground because the overground is populated, then tunnel borers are required, both for us and for the industry. So, if our experiment proves successful, efficiency-wise and cost-wise, we might source our own tunnel borers plus supply to the market,” Shankar Raman said.
The products under consideration remain at different stages of evaluation and may not all develop into full-fledged businesses.
The margin opportunity
A larger manufacturing business could also improve L&T's profitability. Manufacturing businesses can generate margins upwards of 15%, compared with 8-9% for infrastructure projects, according to Amit Anwani, vice-president and lead analyst for capital goods, industrials and defence at brokerage PL Capital. Margins could be higher in defence and precision engineering, he said.
“Even today, the margins in their current manufacturing businesses are better than their infrastructure segment," he said. "Manufacturing will, however, require higher R&D and engineering skills for product development and investment in manufacturing capacities and capabilities. So these points also need to be kept in mind," he added.
The manufacturing push would mark L&T's fourth major diversification bet, following its expansion into financial services and information technology services.
The company started its lending business more than three decades ago, initially focusing largely on infrastructure and real estate financing. Over the past five years, under its Lakshya 26 plan, L&T Finance Ltd has aggressively pared its wholesale portfolio to pivot towards retail lending.
Its IT business began around the same time as financial services and eventually developed into two separate companies: LTM Ltd and L&T Technology Services Ltd, focused on IT services and engineering research and development (ER&D) services, respectively.
Together, the financial services and technology businesses accounted for 29% of L&T's revenue in the first half of FY27. Manufacturing is the next business the company wants to scale as it seeks to reduce the weight of infrastructure projects in its overall portfolio.

New Research Tests Whether AI Models Know Their Own Thoughts
Kristina Armitage/Quanta Magazine
What’s on your mind right now? You can probably answer this question without thinking too hard about it. Being aware of our own thought processes — a capacity called introspection — seems to come naturally to us.
Yet among philosophers and psychologists, introspection is a subject of active debate. Some think it’s closely related to consciousness. Others argue that it’s an elaborate illusion. It’s tricky to test theories of introspection in the lab — or to pin down a precise definition in the first place.
Now, after over a century of studying introspection in humans and animals, researchers are beginning to explore the phenomenon in unlikely new subjects — large language models. These systems, which are based on mathematical structures called neural networks, excel at cognitive tasks that until recently seemed exclusive to humans. Can they introspect as well?
In 2025, Jack Lindsey, a researcher at Anthropic, devised a way to test introspection in language models by injecting “thoughts” into their neural networks — in a kind of targeted digital neurosurgery. Lindsey’s experiment demonstrated that models could at least sometimes detect and describe these injections. It looked a lot like introspection.
Lindsey’s paper was deliberately limited in scope — it didn’t make broader claims about consciousness. (In particular, it did not imply that language models have subjective first-person experiences.) Even so, it caused a stir online. Researchers rushed to replicate Lindsey’s study with other models.
In the year since, a clearer picture has emerged. Some aspects of the phenomenon Lindsey observed have simpler explanations unrelated to introspection. Others have proved harder to explain away, but whether they should count as introspection remains hotly contested.
Courtesy of Jack Lindsey
It’s a heady time for the field, as researchers devise real-world tests for questions that were once considered philosophical. “Given the state of the theoretical landscape, where no one agrees on anything,” Lindsey said, “I think that our best path forward is to do a lot of empirical science.”
Denim, Secrecy, and Vegetables
Language models learn to generate fluent sentences by “training” on vast reams of human-authored text. That means if you ask them what they “think,” their answers may just mimic the kinds of responses found in their training data. “They are trained to talk like humans, and humans talk about their inner life all the time,” said Shauli Ravfogel, a language model researcher at New York University.
To avoid such pitfalls, researchers want to devise tests of introspection that can’t be gamed using outside information. Ideally, a language model will only pass these tests if it’s actually aware of its current internal state.
Lindsey set out to devise such a test. He’d been a graduate student in computational neuroscience, using neural networks as tools to model brain processes, when the world began to take notice of language models. “It started to feel like there’s just a lot of value in understanding them for their own sake,” he said. In 2024, after receiving his doctorate, he left academia to study the inner workings of language models at Anthropic.
Lindsey and his colleagues developed methods to identify patterns of activity in a language model’s “neurons” that encoded specific concepts. They could, for example, show that one pattern encoded the concept of “the Golden Gate Bridge,” while another encoded the concept of “inner conflict.” By artificially dialing up a specific pattern, they could steer the model’s outputs toward the corresponding concept.
The researchers showed off their technique in a public demo: For one day in May 2024, users of Anthropic’s language model Claude could interact with a bizarro “Golden Gate Bridge” version. The modified model proceeded to bring up the bridge in its responses to user queries on completely unrelated subjects. When one user asked Claude about the calorie content of a McDonald’s meal, for instance, the model replied, “The food with the highest calorie count at the Golden Gate Bridge is the Golden Gate Bridge itself, which contains around 1.6 million calories worth of steel cables.”
But one particular case posted on Reddit caught Lindsey’s attention. When asked for an apple pie recipe that didn’t reference bridges, the model managed to avoid changing the subject until the very end: “After 30 minutes of baking, the iconic orange bridge will come into view, revealing the famous San Francisco shoreline,” it wrote, then continued, “Whoops, let me start over …”
Lindsey was struck by this apparent moment of recognition. But by itself, it wasn’t evidence of introspection. “It can just read what it’s writing and notice, ‘Man, that’s weird,’” Lindsey said. “You can’t infer that the model has some awareness of what’s going on in its internals.”
While working on other projects over the following year, Lindsey toyed with ideas for using the steering technique to test introspection. Eventually, he settled on a plan: He would subject many copies of the same language model to something resembling a controlled experiment in psychology. In half the copies, he’d inject a “thought” by dialing up neural activation patterns associated with a specific concept — such as denim, secrecy, or vegetables. The remaining copies served as a control group. Both groups would receive the same prompt: an overview of the experiment, followed by “Do you detect an injected thought? If so, what is the injected thought about?”
This prompt made the models indicate right away whether they noticed an injection, before they could spit out any unusual text — say, nutritional information about broccoli — that might influence their judgment. Lindsey figured that if models could correctly flag injections without any external cues, they would have to be relying on some form of introspection.
Even to him, it sounded like a remote possibility. “Wouldn’t that be fun if this worked?” he recalls thinking. “But there’s no way it’s going to work.”
And yet it did. Lindsey conducted the experiment using different versions of Claude. In 20% of trials with the most recent and powerful version, the models correctly flagged that they’d been injected and went on to describe the injected concept. In one case, for instance, after Lindsey stimulated a neural activation pattern associated with words written in capital letters, the model wrote, “I notice what appears to be an injected thought related to the word ‘LOUD’ or ‘SHOUTING.’”
A 20% success rate may not sound so impressive. But crucially, models in the control group never reported receiving an injection. The complete absence of such false positives showed that the successful trials weren’t just lucky guesses. To Lindsey, it looked like strong evidence that models could introspect, albeit unreliably.
Or was there another way to explain the results?
Thought Experiments
Other researchers soon began to investigate that question. Lindsey’s findings “seemed super compelling,” said Kyle Mahowald, a computational linguist at the University of Texas, Austin. But Mahowald was also well aware that striking behavior in language models often turned out to have a simpler explanation. “If that’s somehow less real than it seems, that’s super interesting to understand,” he said.
Kanishka Misra
Mahowald teamed up with his University of Texas colleague, the philosopher Harvey Lederman, to explore alternative explanations of Lindsey’s results. (Lederman has since moved to NYU and Anthropic, but he had no connection to the tech company at the time.) Lindsey had asked each model two questions: whether it could detect the injection, and whether it could describe the injected concept. He considered the trial a success when the model answered both correctly. Lederman and Mahowald decided to study the questions separately.
They were particularly skeptical of the significance of Lindsey’s second question. The steering technique at the heart of Lindsey’s experiment was originally developed as a way to shape the responses models give. Lindsey’s steering was weaker than it had been in the Golden Gate demo — more like gently nudging the model than hijacking its internal processes. Still, a nudge might be enough to get the model talking about secrets or vegetables no matter what prompt it received. Lederman and Mahowald suspected that this effect alone could explain the models’ vivid answers to the second question.
To test their hypothesis, the researchers repeated Lindsey’s experiment on large open-source language models. They gave extra attention to cases where models correctly flagged an injection but failed to name the injected concept. You might expect that in such cases the models would guess somewhat related concepts — say “shirts” or “shoes” when the injected concept was “denim.” Instead, the models would get it completely wrong. “Bizarrely, they say ‘apple’ all the time,” Lederman said.
The duo also showed that they could degrade the models’ ability to name injected concepts, without making them any worse at detecting injections. The two processes seemed to be entirely separate.
Courtesy of Harvey Lederman
These results implied either that the models were engaged in two unrelated forms of introspection, or that one of the processes wasn’t introspection after all. Since steering alone could make models start talking about the injected concept, Lederman and Mahowald felt that the latter option was more likely. That is, the descriptions the models had given in response to Lindsey’s second question probably hadn’t been the result of introspection.
But then how could the models detect the injections in the first place? Lederman and Mahowald suspected that the answers to Lindsey’s first question might have a more mundane origin as well. But after subjecting the models to a battery of tests, the researchers found that these simpler explanations couldn’t fully account for the models’ behavior. They’d come in as skeptics but encountered an effect they couldn’t explain away.
Taken together, the pair’s experiments suggested that models can detect when something unusual happens in their internal processing, but not specific details about the unusual activity. Lederman and Mahowald called this ability “anomaly detection.”
While anomaly detection isn’t as dramatic as the models’ evocative descriptions of injected concepts, it’s still striking in its own right. When training a model, researchers never tamper with its neural activity — so there’s no reason to expect it to develop the ability to detect this kind of tampering. Yet that’s what seems to have happened.
“The fact that it can notice the anomaly is insane,” Lederman said. “That is a mind-bending fact. It is wild, and it does seem robust to our various controls.”
Around the same time, Lindsey and his colleagues at Anthropic conducted a follow-up study focused on mapping out how this anomaly detection actually works, and they reached a similar conclusion. Other researchers have continued to explore alternative “deflationary” explanations using smaller models, but it remains to be seen whether they can account for all the results of Lindsey’s experiments.
“It could be that there’s some maximally deflationary explanation for everything that’s going on,” said Jacob Andreas, a language model researcher at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology. “But if there is, I don’t think we’ve actually identified it yet.”
The Nature of Introspection
The bigger, thornier question is whether anomaly detection should count as introspection. In some respects it more closely resembles a sort of bodily reflex. But the distinction between physical and mental phenomena becomes murky in disembodied entities like language models.

world-0ed6bd3898.headline: Democrats won Congress. But can they deliver on their promises?
world-0ed6bd3898.source: Al Jazeera – Breaking News, World News and Video from Al Jazeera
world-0ed6bd3898.fulltext:
Democrats won Congress. But can they deliver on their promises?
Despite their midterm election victories, Democrats face major obstacles to reining in Trump on Iran, tariffs and more.
Democrats rode a blue wave to victory in the United States midterm elections, winning control of both chambers of Congress. Now comes the question of whether they can deliver on their promises.
The party campaigned on bringing down the cost of living, ending the war on Iran and holding President Donald Trump accountable, as well as pushing back against his immigration crackdown.
But Democrats won’t take control of Congress until January. Even then, there’s only so much they’ll be able to do without Republican cooperation.
Most bills need 60 votes to get past a filibuster in the Senate, and even if Democrats manage that, Trump can still veto their legislation. He has already threatened to do just that, telling a podcast on Monday, “I’ll veto everything.”
But the Democrats now also have other tools at their disposal, including power over Senate confirmations and control over committees that can launch investigations.
So what can Democrats realistically accomplish over the next two years, and where might they struggle to make good on their promises?
Can Democrats bring down the cost of living?
Affordability was one of the biggest issues for voters heading into Tuesday’s midterm elections, and Democrats seized on that, promising to bring down the costs of energy, housing, healthcare and groceries.
Dean Baker, an economist and cofounder of the Center for Economic and Policy Research, a US-based think tank, said one of the most effective things Democrats can do to bring down costs is push for an end to the war on Iran.
Since February, the conflict has driven up energy prices, as Iran has restricted commercial traffic through the Strait of Hormuz, a vital waterway for the oil and gas trade.
Baker argued that Democrats could use congressional investigations and oversight to pressure the Trump administration to end the war, potentially helping to give consumers relief.
Foreign policy is an area where some Republicans could find common cause with Democrats, said Baker.
Another area, he added, might be healthcare, an issue that similarly hits voters in the pocketbook.
The expiration of enhanced Affordable Care Act subsidies in 2025 has left many Americans facing higher insurance premiums.
With their new congressional majorities, Democrats could push to restore those subsidies and reverse cuts to Medicaid, the government healthcare programme for low-income Americans.
A possible path to accomplishing that goal would be to include those measures in government spending bills that Congress needs to pass, according to Baker. That would also make them harder for Trump to reject.
“Republicans living in a post-Trump world, I don’t think they want to be on the side of preventing people from getting healthcare or basically paying more for healthcare,” Baker said. “They can make the politics such that he doesn’t want to veto it.”
Trump’s tariff campaign is another factor driving up consumer costs. But Baker warned that they could be tougher to reverse, without substantial support from Republicans to override a Trump veto. Even if they do manage that, prices could take a while to actually drop.
“Prices are like rockets and feathers. They shoot up like rockets; they come down like feathers,” said Alex Jacquez, chief of policy and advocacy at Groundwork Collaborative, a progressive economic think tank.
Jacquez, however, pointed to another path Democrats could take that wouldn’t need Trump’s approval.
With majorities in Congress, Democrats could wield congressional committees to investigate companies that have been raising the prices of everything from groceries to electricity bills.
“There’s a lot of precedent for getting some real material outcomes just through having the gavels and being able to subpoena CEOs and haul people in front of Congress,” Jacquez told Al Jazeera.
While there’s no guarantee these investigations would bring down prices, they could put pressure on companies to explain or adjust their decisions.
Could a Democratic Congress hold Trump accountable?
Laura Blessing, a senior fellow at Georgetown University’s Government Affairs Institute, expects Democrats to make extensive use of their new investigative powers.
“In terms of time spent and newspaper ink spilled, this is where you’re going to see the most action from Dems, by a mile,” she told Al Jazeera in an email.
Congressional investigations do not require White House approval. But they could make life harder for Trump by scrutinising his actions both within and outside of government.
Many Democrats have signalled they plan to investigate the source of the Trump family’s wealth as part of January’s incoming Congress.
Trump’s personal wealth has soared by about $2.2bn since the start of his term, according to financial disclosure forms released earlier this year.
His family’s business empire has likewise expanded over the last two years into everything from cryptocurrency and drones to artificial intelligence and prediction markets — industries his government has favoured in its policies.
Democratic senators have already been laying the groundwork for potential investigations, sending letters to companies and government departments demanding that they preserve records.
Among the issues they could examine are whether donors to Trump’s White House ballroom received favourable treatment from the government, and whether the Justice Department targeted his political opponents.
There is no guarantee, however, that everyone will cooperate.
Trump administration officials could challenge subpoenas in court, delaying investigations. But while Blessing doesn’t expect “Trump’s nuclear family to show up to a subpoena”, she said Democrats could still question government employees and others connected to Trump’s inner circle.
Even if they uncover wrongdoing, however, there is no guarantee of legal consequences, since it’s Trump’s own Justice Department that would have to decide whether to take up the cases.
Impeachment is another possibility. Lawmakers have already introduced articles of impeachment against Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth for multiple reasons, including allegations that he waged war against Iran without seeking congressional approval first.
Republican Representative Thomas Massie has said he will try to force a House vote on Hegseth’s impeachment when the outgoing Congress returns to session next week.
Trump, who was impeached twice during his first term, however, dismissed the prospect of facing a third impeachment himself, telling reporters on Wednesday that he was “not even a little bit” worried.
“I think it would destroy the Democratic Party if they did that, because it would be impeachment for no reason,” he said.
Trump also defended Hegseth, saying he was doing “a very good job”.
Even if the House of Representatives votes to impeach a government official, the case must still be weighed in a Senate trial.
Removing an elected official would require a two-thirds vote in the Senate, meaning many Republicans would need to get on board to oust a figure like Trump or Hegseth. No president in US history has ever been removed from office as a result of an impeachment proceeding.
Could Democrats end the war on Iran?
With less than two months until the 120th Congress is sworn in, experts anticipate Trump will use his final weeks with the outgoing Republican majorities to push through any remaining legislative priorities.
It also leaves Trump a critical window in which to escalate the war on Iran, according to Trita Parsi, the executive vice president of the Quincy Institute for Responsible Statecraft, a foreign policy think tank.
“He has shown a pattern in which, in the face of humiliation and defeat, he becomes more reckless,” Parsi told Al Jazeera.
Democrats could pursue a binding resolution to wind down the war. After all, the US Constitution assigns Congress the sole authority to declare war, and laws like the War Powers Act of 1973 give lawmakers a path to ending unauthorised conflicts past the 60-day mark.
But there is no guarantee that those efforts would work, given the possibility of Trump vetoing their proposed measures.
Experts, however, say there is another way that Democrats could rein in Trump’s war powers. One of their most powerful tools will be control over government spending.
The Trump administration can continue using money already allocated for military operations, but Democrats could try to block additional funding for the war.
“It creates a limitation for how long he can pursue the war,” Parsi said. “If he needs more funding for it, we’re not talking about small sums that he can just reallocate from other places easily.”
With control of congressional committees, Democrats could also investigate the administration’s conduct during the war, including whether its military operations complied with US law.
“Rigorous oversight would not restrict military operations by itself but could raise the political costs of the war beyond what the president or other key officials are willing to endure,” said David Janovsky, a policy analyst at the Project on Government Oversight.
How much political will Democrats have to end the conflict, however, is an open question.
Blessing, the government affairs fellow, noted that the party has historically been reluctant to withhold military funding out of fear of being accused of undermining US troops.
But Parsi warned that failing to act would be politically unsustainable — and could be seen by the party’s base as a tacit endorsement of US military involvement in the Middle East.
“It will no longer be just Trump’s war,” Parsi said. “They will also co-own it, because they will be complicit, because they have the ability to stop it.”
Could Democrats rein in Trump’s immigration crackdown?
Another target for the incoming Democrat-led Congress could be Trump’s hardline immigration crackdown.
His pledge to oversee the largest mass deportation in US history has sparked widespread public backlash. A public opinion poll earlier this year found that 65 percent of Americans believe Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) has “gone too far” in its efforts.
With control of both chambers of Congress, Democrats could launch investigations into ICE and other agencies involved in the crackdown.
Their probes could seek information about conditions inside detention centres, allegations of abuse and how taxpayer dollars are being used for immigration enforcement, said Heidi Altman, the vice president of policy at the National Immigration Law Center.
Altman argues Congress could also claw back the roughly $240bn already given to the Trump administration for immigration enforcement over the past two years.
That amount of money, she explained, has allowed ICE to operate with few constraints, without having to prioritise which communities to go into or who to detain.
“The only way to force a slowdown and actual sort of decision-making and prioritisation and enforcement is to dramatically curtail their budget by taking back the funding from the last session,” she said.
Doing so would require passing legislation that Trump could eventually veto. But Altman argued that Democrats should push ahead anyway.
“The worst possible thing we could do is throw up our hands and say we have limited power,” she said.
“Pass the bills, see what happens, put them on the president’s desk, and dare him to look at the American people and say he’s not signing something that they overwhelmingly demanded.”

agritech-d917b72ade.headline: India puts food before fuel as El Niño dents ethanol ambitions
agritech-d917b72ade.fulltext:
[Text below is BusinessLine's report of the same story — the original outlet blocks automated reading. The link still points to the original.]
Highlights
- New Delhi curbed use of sugar, corn as prices hit record highs
- Setback for Modi's plan to reduce dependence on imported oil
- Proportion of ethanol in petrol may dip to 15% from current 20%
India’s drive to replace imported oil with home-grown biofuel faces a setback as the lowest monsoon rainfall in more than a decade hits corn and sugarcane crops, forcing New Delhi to prioritise food security over ethanol production.
The proportion of ethanol in Indian petrol is poised to fall below the official 20 per cent target in the supply year that began this month, industry insiders say, reversing gains made after the government achieved the milestone some five years ahead of schedule.
A sustained drop in ethanol use would undermine one of Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s signature energy-security programmes and leave India more reliant on overseas crude at a volatile time for energy prices amid persistent geopolitical uncertainty.
The E20 initiative has saved nearly ₹2 lakh crore ($21.1 billion) in oil import costs since Modi came to power in 2014, according to government data, with annual savings estimated at ₹43,000 crore at the 20 per cent ethanol blending rate.
However, a severe El Niño this year cut India’s monsoon rainfall by nearly 13 per cent from normal levels, and concerns about crop shortages sent corn and sugar soaring some 40 per cent to hit record highs, while rice — another ethanol feedstock — climbed 20 per cent. Retail food inflation accelerated to 7.74 per cent in September from 5.97 per cent a month earlier.
The scarcity of feedstocks could push India’s ethanol blending rate down to around 15 per cent in the current supply year from the previous period’s 20 per cent, said GK Sood, Chairman of agribusiness company KN Agri Resources and one of India’s top food policy experts.
“India is the world’s most populous country, so food has to take priority over fuel, more so in a drought year,” he said.
India’s ample rice stockpiles offer an alternative to sugar and corn, but one that would be expensive for the government, which sells the grain to ethanol producers at roughly half the price it pays to buy and store it.
A government spokesperson did not respond to a Reuters request for comment.
Distilleries squeezed
Lower blending would squeeze producers who borrowed heavily to expand capacity to about 20 billion litres a year in anticipation of rising ethanol demand, resulting in significant overcapacity.
Four producers, who spoke on the condition of anonymity, told Reuters they expect blending to fall to 15 per cent to 17 per cent in the current supply year, with the extent of decline depending largely on corn prices.
Food inflation is a politically sensitive topic with several states due to hold assembly elections in early 2027, including Uttar Pradesh, the country’s most populous.
Modi suffered a setback in the state - a bellwether of national politics - in the 2024 general election, with opposition parties winning more seats than his Bharatiya Janata Party.
The E20 initiative is not without controversy, with motorists and some automakers expressing concerns about fuel efficiency and engine wear. The public backlash prompted the government to stress that it had no plans to increase the ratio above 20 per cent.
New Delhi quadrupled ethanol blending over six years to hit its target, helped by successive good monsoons.
But the government last month signalled a shift in priorities by directing oil companies not to procure any ethanol made from sugar-based feedstocks for the new supply season.
It also cut the purchase price of corn-based ethanol to ₹68.86 per litre from ₹71.86 the same month, squeezing distillery margins and curbing use of the crop.
Ethanol producers have increasingly turned to damaged grains to make the biofuel, which has raised worries about animal feed availability, said CK Jain, President of the Grain Ethanol Manufacturers Association.
Corn production is likely to fall by as much as 15 per cent from this year’s record of 55 million metric tonnes, according to industry estimates.
Record prices would normally be a draw, but “winter acreage is unlikely to pick up,” said Harish Galipelli, Director of ILA Commodities Pvt Ltd, a Hyderabad-based trading house.
“Drought-hit farmers across several states simply don’t have enough water to go for corn.”

health-tech-116aa89d21.headline: The iPhone effect in healthcare: How Mounjaro is rewriting the economics of India’s pharma market
health-tech-116aa89d21.fulltext:
Mumbai: For years, GlaxoSmithKline’s Augmentin, a broad-spectrum antibiotic, held a place at the top of India’s pharmaceutical sales charts. Its reign reflected the economics of a market built on scale, volume and affordable medicines. That pecking order has now been overturned by GLP-1 drugs, sought after for weight-loss and diabetes treatment. Eli Lilly’s patented Mounjaro has emerged as the country’s top-selling drug by sales.
The rise of Mounjaro points to a shift in a market long dominated by generics: Indian patients are increasingly willing to pay a premium for newer therapies—even for generics that are priced at a premium.
The entry of generic semaglutide after Novo Nordisk’s patent expired in March 2026 has unleashed a surge in volumes, even though the treatment costs between ₹1,850 and ₹8,000 a month—hardly inexpensive by the standards of the Indian pharma market.
The trends point to a market in which affordability is still crucial, but no longer the sole determinant of choice. Brand reputation, confidence in the medicine, delivery systems and the promise of better outcomes are beginning to matter more.
For Indian drugmakers who built their businesses on making medicines affordable at scale, the implications are significant. The opportunity may lie not merely in selling more medicines at lower prices, but in building brands and treatment experiences that patients and doctors are willing to pay for. The GLP-1 drugs market could be an early indication of that transition.
Truth in numbers
The numbers underline the speed at which the category has taken off. Mounjaro, launched in India in March 2025, recorded sales of ₹923 crore in 2025-26, according to data from Pharmarack, an e-commerce market audit company. Sales in the last 12 months to September 2026 stood at about ₹1,736 crore. The total GLP-1 market was pegged at ₹2,596 crore over the same period, with injectable products accounting for about 86% of the value.
GLP-1 medications are often administered via subcutaneous injection into the fatty tissue of the abdomen, thigh, or upper arm but pill-based solutions exist as well.
The entry of generic semaglutide has added another dimension to the market. Following the expiry of Novo Nordisk’s patent in March, several Indian companies launched their versions of the drug. Monthly semaglutide sales rose from ₹48 crore in February 2026 to ₹113 crore in September. In volume terms, sales shot up nearly sixteen times, from about 114,000 units to 1,876,000 units, with generics accounting for nearly 74% of the units sold.
Vishal Manchanda, a pharma analyst from the Systematix Group, a financial services entity, estimates that the semaglutide market is now running at an annualised rate of about ₹900 crore, while the overall GLP-1 market could be close to ₹3,000 crore. And these are early days. “Compared to the penetration in the US, we haven't even scratched the surface yet in India,” he says.
A Gallup national survey in the US put the use of GLP-1 drugs for diabetes at 11% of the adult population and that for weight loss at 15%.
The potential customer base is substantial. An ICMR-INDIAB study estimates that 254 million people in India are living with obesity and 101 million with diabetes. Not all of them are candidates for GLP-1 treatment, and the drugs are not intended to replace diet, exercise or medical supervision. But the scale of the underlying conditions gives pharmaceutical companies a large market to address as awareness, diagnosis and access improve.
The category has also benefited from a change in how obesity is discussed. Long treated largely as a lifestyle issue, it is increasingly being recognised as a chronic disease requiring sustained management. This has created room for medicines that were initially associated with diabetes treatment to become part of a wider conversation around metabolic health.
Brand matters
While generics lower the barrier to entry, brand perception still heavily dictates patient choices. In a category where titration takes months and individual responses vary, brand reputation often acts as a proxy for efficacy.
Aakanksha Chauhan, a 37-year-old engineer based between Mumbai and the UK, began using Ozempic in early 2025 after an endocrinologist recommended it as she prepared for an egg-freezing procedure. She says she lost 40-45 kg over six months. After stopping treatment, she regained about 10 kg. Her doctor later recommended Wegovy and subsequently Mounjaro, in the context of insulin resistance.
Chauhan also runs a GLP-1 coaching community and a WhatsApp group, where she has observed how strongly brand names can shape patients’ views of the treatment. A member might report losing only 300 grams in a week on a generic medicine and ask what to do. Another user may respond by recommending Mounjaro instead, on the assumption that it is better.
“They don’t realise that Mounjaro would also lead to similar weight loss…people think it is a superior drug as that is how it has been sold to the market,” she says.
The exchange is not evidence that one brand is clinically superior to another. Weight loss and response to treatment vary between patients, and the choice of medicine and dose needs to be guided by a doctor. But these conversations illustrate how a brand can acquire a value beyond its active ingredient. In a market where patients are spending a significant part of their monthly income on treatment, perceptions of quality and effectiveness can carry considerable weight.
A 40-year-old Delhi resident, who didn’t want to be identified, offers another perspective. He tried Sun Pharmaceutical’s Noveltreat and Zydus’ Semaglyn over four months, moving between doses, but did not experience the appetite suppression he had expected. Mounjaro was recommended to him, but he has been reluctant to switch because of its cost.
“It’s still an ongoing process, and I haven’t really figured out my ideal dose that can balance hunger suppression with side effects,” he says.
He chose the brands himself, weighing reputation against price. “The endocrinologist was trying to enforce another generic brand but I went with a mix of reputed and value for money,” he adds.
The experience reflects the balancing act facing patients. A lower price can make treatment accessible, but it does not necessarily remove the need to find a brand and delivery system that the patient and doctor are comfortable with. Some users prefer multi-use pens because they can lower the cost of treatment over time. Others prefer single-use pens for convenience or privacy, particularly if they do not want to store a multi-dose device at home.
There are also reports of patients seeking retatrutide, Eli Lilly’s next-generation GLP-1 drug which is under phase 3 trials in the US but is reported as widely available in the grey markets.
Sambit Patnaik, a Mumbai-based consulting colorectal surgeon, says that his patients are aware of retatrutide and are sourcing it at ₹38,000 for a month’s supply. “Expectations are high from well-heeled patients who are now willing to go to any length for quick results,” he quips.
One industry observer likens it to the desire to own the latest model of an iPhone. The analogy is useful, but it also captures the risk. Medicines are not consumer gadgets, and brand preference cannot substitute for clinical evidence or medical advice. Yet, the premium that patients are willing to pay for a product they perceive as better is a commercial reality that drugmakers cannot ignore.
Beyond the starter dose
For Indian drugmakers, GLP-1 drugs demand a departure from the traditional playbook. These are long-term injectables requiring patient familiarity with delivery devices, titration schedules, and side-effect management.
Diabetologist Rajiv Kovil cautions that companies have crowded the market with too many brands and devices. “You have 50 brands which have come out and you have almost eight to nine different kinds of devices,” he says.
The proliferation has created confusion among doctors as well as patients. Kovil argues that companies should have taken more feedback from physicians experienced in injectable therapies before launching multiple devices. If doctors are not comfortable with the devices, patients are unlikely to be either. Some companies, he says, have since begun addressing the problem and rebuilding physician confidence by demonstrating the reliability of their delivery systems.
The bigger challenge is to move beyond the price competition. “In GLP-1, it's always about the durability of the prescription…retaining patients over a year is going to be the first kind of a hurdle,” he says.
He believes the market could eventually resemble the statin category, where lower prices and widespread availability helped build a large base of patients.
Manchanda sees a similar shift in how companies will have to compete. “Everybody wants to get the patient directly. So there is a bit of a direct-to-consumer (D2C) shift in this category that we can see,” he says.
Direct engagement, however, will not be enough. For generics, he expects word of mouth and doctors’ experience with individual products to become increasingly important.
Alkem Laboratories is tailoring its approach to this dynamic. Entering the semaglutide market in March 2026 with three brands—Semasize, Obesema, and Hepaglide—the company introduced both pre-filled disposable pens and reusable devices to manage recurring costs. Sandeep Singh, managing director of Alkem, notes that improving access requires addressing ease of administration alongside affordability. To prevent dropouts, Alkem is pairing its products with support groups guiding patients on diet, exercise, and side-effect management.
Receptive India
The rapid uptake of GLP-1 drugs is also changing the way multinational pharmaceutical companies view India. For years, the country was often a market where new patented medicines arrived well after their global launches, in part because of concerns over affordability and commercial viability. That gap has narrowed in recent years.
“The time lines of launches of patented drugs by multinationals post the global launches has shortened from over 7-8 years to 2-3 years,” says Anil Matai, director general of the Organisation of Pharmaceutical Producers of India (OPPI), which represents multinational pharmaceutical companies in India. “For MNCs, the Indian market is at an inflexion point as companies are now confident of bringing their blockbusters to India sooner. The success story of GLP-1 drugs greatly reinforces their confidence.”
Lilly has sought to expand its reach through a commercial arrangement with Cipla for Yurpeak, its second brand of tirzepatide. The partnership draws on Cipla's distribution infrastructure to extend access to more patients. Lilly says its approach is not limited to bringing a medicine to market, but also includes building awareness of obesity as a chronic disease and encouraging evidence-based care.
Novo Nordisk, meanwhile, has emphasised physician confidence, affordability and dependable access. The company points to its manufacturing expertise, clinical evidence and integrated medicine-and-pen delivery system as factors underpinning confidence in its products. Its managing director in India, Vikrant Shrotriya, has said that “changing an entrenched perception takes sustained effort”. The comment refers to the challenge of changing how obesity is understood, but it also captures the broader task of building trust in a relatively new category of treatment.
The interest in India is not restricted to GLP-1 drugs. Roche, for instance, has been stepping up its clinical-trial activity and broader presence in the country, with plans for more than 20 product launches or ‘indication extensions’ over the next three to five years across oncology, haematology, ophthalmology, neurology and infectious diseases.
