work-careers-5b3e720de3.headline: Am I going to be fired by AI? How corporate America is being seduced by AI and algorithms in the ‘forever layoffs’ era
work-careers-5b3e720de3.fulltext:
For five years, the former Meta employee had been feted as a high performer by her managers. She had even received a rare equity award in recognition of her performance, which had never fallen below an “exceeds expectations” rating.
Imagine her surprise, then, when she was unceremoniously laid off this past spring.
Perhaps she should have seen the writing on the wall. After she took a medical leave in late 2025, her performance rating slipped. It turned out she’d initially been given an “exceeds expectations” rating, but her manager had been forced to change her rating to fit a bell curve. Her job responsibilities also changed substantially. She had always ranked high on the internal dashboards Meta used to track AI adoption, which categorized its most avid practitioners as “AI first” or “AI native.” But after returning, she noticed her scores had dropped and was startled to realize the dashboards had not taken into account that she was on protected leave.
Another employee impacted by the layoffs, a former director at Meta, had come to a similar conclusion. He monitored his team’s usage of artificial intelligence closely, almost on a daily basis, and noticed the dashboards had “failed to distinguish employees’ leave from lack of engagement,” as he said in recent legal filings. In other words, there was no way to detect if someone’s ranking had been compromised simply because they were on leave.
In an era of forever layoffs, some tech workers have suspected that an algorithm or AI could be responsible for picking off employees. Now, it seems, those fears may be realized, as captured by a novel lawsuit that the Meta employees brought in July, alongside a number of former colleagues who were also laid off this year. The 26 anonymous plaintiffs made a bold claim: They accused Meta of using AI-enabled systems to determine which employees would be laid off in a major round of cuts this year—and that, as a result, the company had disproportionately targeted people who needed accommodations for disabilities or took parental leave.
Job displacement isn’t the only consequence of widespread AI adoption. A Fast Company LinkedIn poll reveals . . .
that the fears of being ousted by AI are palpable, and not just for disgruntled tech workers. More than two-thirds of people surveyed said they were worried about their company deploying AI to select employees for layoffs. Of more than 480 respondents, 37% said they were “very” concerned about the prospect of AI being used to that end.
For months, Meta has strenuously denied the claims laid out in the lawsuit, insisting humans were involved throughout the layoff selection process. In one declaration, Linh Doan, an HR leader, stressed that “AI did not select anyone for termination. AI did not assist anyone in making selection decisions.”
But those kinds of proclamations may be too little, too late. Workers know their employers already use automated tools to collect all kinds of data that informs hiring and promotion decisions. Major companies like JPMorgan Chase, Disney, and, of course, Meta are now enlisting AI to draft self-assessments and performance reviews. People analytics tools often track absenteeism and sick days, an exercise in productivity theater that employers nonetheless use to evaluate worker output—even though relying on that kind of data could harm people who take leave.
So it’s not hard to imagine that all this data could influence layoff decisions, as companies are armed with more information on their employees than ever before. Some managers and HR leaders have said as much in anonymous surveys, where they admit to using AI to trim head count. A handful of states have already passed legislation that will force companies to be more transparent about how AI factors into termination decisions, in anticipation of the potential impact on workers. Meanwhile, high-profile lawsuits against HR tech companies like Workday and Eightfold indicate that we are just beginning to understand how AI use could perpetuate discrimination in other stages of the employment cycle.
As AI becomes more pervasive across corporate America, it is increasingly difficult for workers to assess the extent to which it may be used in layoff decisions and how all the data companies are hoovering up could be wielded against them. Perhaps the real concern is not whether AI is conducting layoffs—but that there is so little visibility into how AI is radically transforming the way companies make decisions about their workforce.
The precedent for automating layoffs
As companies ramp up pressure on employees to adopt AI, and layoffs become a regular feature across workplaces, it seems only natural that the technology may start to influence how companies approach some of the most difficult decisions they have to make about their workforce.
“Making layoff decisions is an impossible problem because you are not only getting rid of people, but you’re also changing the structure of the work itself in ways that are very hard to predict,” says Richard Landers, a professor of industrial and organizational psychology at the University of Minnesota. “It makes using external tools very attractive [because] some of that responsibility is offloaded.”
While there is limited evidence that large employers are explicitly using AI tools to generate lists of employees to lay off, the idea of productivity metrics or automated systems driving employment decisions is hardly new.
“There has always been to a degree some form of measurement, explicit or implicit, that goes into layoffs,” says Joseph Fuller, a Harvard Business School professor of management. He points to the layoffs Ford conducted in the 1970s by asking supervisors which employees were most productive or spent more hours in the office—the type of metrics companies can now easily monitor through swipe card data or email traffic analysis. “Using AI to make those decisions is really in its infancy,” he says.
Warehouse workers are already subject to more monitoring and can automatically lose their jobs for not meeting productivity quotas at companies like Amazon. Gig workers at Uber and DoorDash can be automatically suspended or find their accounts deactivated with little human oversight; in fact, Uber is facing a fine of nearly $1 billion in the Netherlands for suspending drivers (though the company plans to appeal).
White-collar workplaces track such data points as sick days and other absences to measure absenteeism, even keeping tabs on disengaged employees who might be a “flight risk.” The COVID-19 pandemic and rise of remote work prompted some companies—among them JPMorgan Chase—to more closely monitor how their employees spent their time, tracking keyboard activity and meeting cadence to evaluate productivity. A New York Times report from 2022 found that eight of the 10 largest private employers in the country collected productivity data on their workers.
In 2025, the Department of Government Efficiency sought to automate layoffs across the government while making sweeping cuts to the federal workforce. A Reuters report revealed that DOGE revived an old piece of software called AutoRIF, which the government had developed decades before in an attempt to automate layoffs. The tool was deemed too “clunky” to actually use, according to Reuters.
But DOGE reportedly tapped a Tesla engineer to redesign the software to identify federal workers for layoffs, renaming it the “Workforce Reshaping Tool” and disseminating it to federal agencies for testing. (It’s not clear whether the software was involved in making cuts to the federal workforce—or whether AI was used for layoffs in any capacity.)
Multiple experts told Fast Company there are no tools on the market that are expressly designed to conduct layoffs, and in states like California, there are laws in place to govern how companies use AI or automated systems for employment decisions. But that could change soon.
A VC funding flood
In the first quarter of 2026, AI companies reportedly received more than 80% of overall venture capital funding—something like $242 billion—which means plenty of new tools could emerge on the scene. And some companies may simply position their tools in a manner that evades scrutiny. One researcher told Fast Company they had recently approached a people analytics provider to partner on a study examining AI-driven layoffs. The company—which the researcher described as a market leader—ultimately declined to participate because its software and AI-driven products were being branded as workforce management tools, with the implicit acknowledgement that “workforce management is code for layoffs.”
Once AI becomes embedded in virtually every workflow, it is perhaps unavoidable that termination decisions will draw on inputs from automated systems. In the near future, asking whether AI was involved in the process, as Fuller puts it, “will be the equivalent of saying: ‘Did you use any data in this decision?’”
As workforce management tools grow more sophisticated, companies will likely turn to AI and automation to evaluate individual employees in the context of layoffs. One way employers are already using AI to make cuts, however, is in the context of broader changes to their workforce as they eliminate job functions “in one fell swoop,” according to Fuller.
“Companies are beginning to understand what the first generation of agents can do, and that’s causing them to start adjusting workforces,” he adds. “It’s not so much that they’re doing the layoff because they’ve analyzed individual workers’ performance using AI. It’s because they’ve made a judgment about the durability of an existing job description in light of AI.”
The influence of “work intelligence tools”
Some employers are more and more interested in what the Gartner analyst Emily Rose McRae describes as “work intelligence tools,” which are effectively designed to meet this current moment. McRae says these tools claim they can identify which jobs will be most exposed to AI at a given company. “The phrase usually used is ‘impacted,’ or where there is ‘opportunity,’” she explains, “by which they mean where they think you could replace head count.”
In practice, however, these tools—which McRae says some companies are using to determine which jobs should be cut—are not very good at taking into account all the variables that influence whether a job can truly be supplanted with AI, echoing the concerns many economists have expressed.
“It’s appealing to have an external party say, ‘Here’s what the impact will be,’” she says. “It doesn’t feel as personal.”
Large employers tend to have access to more robust tools—whether developed internally or acquired through third-party vendors—as well as legal teams that should, in theory, ensure layoffs don’t inadvertently target specific groups of employees. The concern at smaller or midsize companies is that managers may get limited guidance on layoff decisions or lack access to enterprise grade tools, leaving them to seek out informal help from chatbots like Claude or Copilot.
“A veneer of objectivity”
Hatim Rahman, a management and organizations professor at Northwestern University, is not surprised to hear that managers are using AI or related tools to make difficult termination decisions. “AI and algorithms give a veneer of objectivity,” he says. “Numbers can be very seductive in providing justification for why certain people can be laid off. The problem is that many times the people who are making decisions about layoffs don’t have an understanding of how the AI tools or workforce analytics that are being used are generating those recommendations or that data.”
If a hiring manager inputs performance review data and asks for layoff recommendations, for example, the chatbot may not consider whether the reviews are capturing the right metrics in the first place. “The thing that’s new is that anybody can do this, which means they don’t have to have any understanding of human

other-interests-41a5428cc5.headline: Wearable device makers are harvesting brain data to train AI—without telling users
other-interests-41a5428cc5.fulltext:
This story was produced in partnership with the Pulitzer Center’s AI Accountability Network.
Half an hour before bed, Adnan Jinnah sits on a chair and straps on a headband. It looks like something a tennis player might wear, save for a large rectangular button on the front. When he feels ready to sleep, he lies down, presses the button, and starts an app on his phone. “That’s pretty much it,” he says.
As he sleeps, sensors in the device pick up Jinnah’s brain activity, heart rate, and blood flow and oxygen to his brain. The signals are then interpreted by algorithms that spit out data on his sleep quality that he can look at in the morning.
The device, known as a Muse headband, was developed by the Canadian consumer neurotechnology company Interaxon. On and off for more than 4 years Jinnah, who lives in Leicester, England, has had trouble falling asleep. He says daily reports from the device allow him to monitor how well he slept the night before and how poor sleep affects his mood. It also provides him with long-term data about his sleep that have helped him understand how different factors, including medication or stress, can influence his rest.
What Jinnah didn’t know, however, was that data from his headband may have been feeding an artificial intelligence (AI) model of the brain. Interaxon is building the model—known in the industry as a “brain foundation model”—to sharpen its picture of how the brain works, especially during sleep and times of focus. The company says this would allow it to provide a better service to its users and develop a product to help support brain research. The data used to train it are overwhelmingly coming from users like Jinnah.
So far, Interaxon has trained its model on about 50,000 hours of electroencephalography (EEG) data from users of the technology, the company says. The data are stripped of personal details, such as people’s names and emails. The company plans to keep expanding this figure. “We aim to use as much of that eligible corpus as possible,” says Chief Marketing Officer Nadia Kumentas.
For Jinnah and potentially tens of thousands of other Muse users like him, it was too little too late: The training had already happened, without his explicit informed consent. When user data get embedded into an AI system they are near-impossible to remove.
Jinnah felt a sense of “resignation” when Science told him his neural data may have been used to train an AI system that he had never heard about. “I suppose it’s very similar to when big tech companies consume your data.” But he thought users should be asked for their consent.
Interaxon is not unusual. In a yearlong investigation, Science reviewed dozens of consumer neurotech privacy policies and spoke to neurotech experts, companies, and users to understand how consumers’ brain data are being used around the world. The investigation reveals a largely unregulated global ecosystem in which tens of millions of hours of EEG data have already been collected by consumer neurotech companies. Multiple firms are using these data in the race to build a brain foundation model.
The findings come as researchers and policymakers argue that the massive accumulation of brain data constitutes a broader privacy risk. Multilateral organizations such as UNESCO and the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development have recently highlighted the rise of consumer-grade brain-computer interfaces as a special concern. In October, United Nations Secretary-General António Guterres presented a report warning that the rapid development of neurotechnologies could give governments access to our innermost thoughts, posing a threat to human rights.
Some experts argue that because consumer neurotechnology devices don’t collect clinical-grade data, it’s unlikely that companies—or governments with access to the data—can glean much about users. But most agree that users have the right to know how their neural data are being used, and that more needs to be done to protect the data.
“Brain signals aren’t heartbeats. Monitoring them is meaningfully different,” says Owen Jones, professor of law and biological sciences at Vanderbilt University. “We are the sum of our brain’s activities in a way that we are never the sum of our other organs’ functions.”
Over the past decade, wearable neurotechnologies have caught on around the world. Consumers can buy devices that promise to monitor stress, fatigue, focus, sleep, meditative states, and more from a growing number of companies. The neurotechnology market value is also steadily on the rise: It is estimated at about $19.19 billion this year and expected to reach nearly $33 billion by 2034. Recently, tech giants have also entered the arena. In 2023, Apple filed a patent for earbuds that could collect EEG data. And last year, Meta launched its Neural Band, which collects data on tiny electrical signals from wrist muscles.
The majority of these wearable neurotechnologies are stripped-down versions of EEG headsets commonly used in hospitals. Clinical-grade headsets tend to gather data using 19 to 25 electrodes spaced across the skull, but brain wearables usually have between one and six. These generally cover a limited part of a person’s brain region—for example, the front of the head or around the ears—depending on what the device is meant to track.
Although some devices have been rigorously tested and used in thousands of scientific studies, the vast majority lack scientific underpinning. One study published in 2018 examined the scientific evidence behind claims made by consumer EEG companies that providing people with real-time information about their brain waves can help them improve their concentration, sleep, and other behaviors. Of more than 3000 publications cited by these companies, only 11 used gold-standard research methods, and 10 of these found no real benefits compared with a control condition.
Because consumer-oriented devices tend to be lighter, simpler, and more user-friendly than clinical tools, the quality of the data is often compromised. EEG is also inherently limited. It’s great for understanding when brain activity takes place, but not for telling you exactly where, particularly when the activity originates in deeper parts of the brain, such as the amygdala, hippocampus, or thalamus, which play important roles in emotion, memory, and sensory processing. As such, some experts say that although brain data collected by consumer devices might reveal broad changes in neural activity, such as when someone falls asleep, they can’t reveal much about a person’s mental state.
But although EEG might not read people’s thoughts, “it would be equally misleading to suggest that it cannot reveal meaningful information about their cognitive states,” says Pietro Aricò, professor of bioengineering at the Sapienza University of Rome. And as consumer EEG devices begin to incorporate AI and are able to conduct increasingly sophisticated analyses, data collected on the outer surface of the brain could be enough to decode intimate features of our mental lives, including our thoughts, emotions, and personality, says Rafael Yuste, co-founder of the Neurorights Foundation, a nonprofit dedicated to protecting people’s brain data rights.
For the companies that make these devices, the data are gold, and they have amassed millions of hours of them. They are used to train algorithms, help companies offer personalized insights to users, and generate evidence they can use to market their products. “Our brain data is the most valuable part of the company,” Kumentas says.
Increasingly, brain data are valued for a specific purpose: training AI brain models. In many ways these models are analogous to large language models such as ChatGPT or Claude, but they are trained on neural data rather than text. After being fed an enormous amount of data, a model recognizes key patterns of brain activity. Researchers can then easily adapt this model to perform different tasks, such as identifying patterns associated with sleep or neurological conditions. The goal is to build a flexible model of the brain that can be used for various tasks with little or no additional training.
The companies building these models believe they could become a breakthrough technology, by helping researchers better understand how the brain works and automating some doctors’ tasks so they can focus on more critical work. “The model is there in order to serve the world for so many things,” said Tan Le, founder and CEO of Emotiv, a San Francisco–based neurotech startup that has developed multiple EEG wearables.
These models are still at a relatively early stage. But they have already shown promise. The AI neurotech startup Piramidal, for instance, has developed a brain foundation model using EEG data from publicly available sources and hospital partnerships, rather than consumer devices. Last year, the startup partnered with the Cleveland Clinic to develop a way to automatically detect seizures in hospital patients. After the model was fine-tuned on the clinic’s library of seizure-related EEG data, it correctly identified nine out of 10 seizures in a pilot study.
Some experts say these models may be useful in specific cases, but doubt that an all-encompassing AI brain model is feasible—particularly one relying on consumer data. It would have to generalize across different kinds of brain states, diseases, and populations—from people with Parkinson’s disease all the way to paralyzed patients wanting to communicate. “It’s still a very, very long way off,” says Adam Caplan, founder and general partner at Jumpspace Ventures, a venture capital firm focusing on neurotechnologies.
He and others say building such a model would require high-quality data that consumer neurotechnology devices often do not collect. Yet nine consumer neurotechnology and AI software companies have publicly acknowledged building a brain foundation model, and others may be doing so quietly.
Similar concerns arise when companies exploit data from other sources. Piramidal has trained its model on more than 4 million hours of EEG data from open-source data sets and partnerships with hospitals and institutions. “We did these automated searches on the internet in order to find publicly available and curated data that is not proprietary,” says Dimitris Fotis Sakellariou, the company’s founder and CEO.
These include sources such as Temple University’s EEG Corpus, which contains 60,000 recordings, including seizure-related data, and is open to researchers. Participants in such studies consent to providing their data for research, but neuroethicists warn they are unlikely to have envisioned their data being used to train sophisticated AI brain models. “It matters if you agree to something and then there’s a totally different context of use that you never contemplated,” says Nita Farahany, professor of law and philosophy at Duke University.
But Sakalleriou argues people participating in these studies are precisely the kinds of patients who want to see brain foundation models come to life. “I have spent a lot of time in hospitals, and I can tell you for a fact that these people that gave consent for their EEGs are waiting for something to be built like that.”
It’s not just how data are used, but where they might end up that raises concerns. Of those companies with privacy policies, all except one allow data to be shared with third parties in anonymized, aggregated, or deidentified forms, although they often do not specify whether this includes brain data. Only six explicitly stated they would not sell the user’s brain data, although another 17 state in general terms that they don’t sell or trade personal information. All companies reviewed either explicitly permitted data to be shared with authorities—including police, government, or courts—upon request, or did not specify.

other-interests-ab9b25b62f.fulltext:
To say that someone has ‘good hands’ is high praise in a molecular biology laboratory, where researchers must deftly handle delicate glassware, pipette samples and more. But in an unusual genetics lab at Shanghai Jiao Tong University in China, a team of robots driven by artificial intelligence is designing and doing experiments with no hands to speak of.
Inside the ‘self-driving’ lab revolutio
The facility, described today1 in Nature, is one of the latest steps towards ‘self-driving’ labs that are guided by AI, with minimal input from human scientists. With samples moved around by robotic arms, the Shanghai lab can operate more than 20 types of instrument, complete thousands of operations in a single project and do experiments that involve synthesizing and sequencing DNA, among other tasks.
An experiment is designed and executed from start to finish by a team of AI agents, following a simple prompt from a human operator. After that, human hands are needed only to refresh reagents and to service hardware.
The system, called AutoDNA, is remarkable both for its degree of autonomy and because it can readily incorporate a diverse range of lab equipment, says Milad Abolhasani, a chemical engineer at North Carolina State University in Raleigh. “The future of science is going to involve a lot of autonomous labs.”
On autopilot
Labs have long incorporated automation into their workflows, using machines to conduct specific aspects of experimental protocols, such as mixing and heating chemicals. Now, some researchers are hoping to harness increasingly sophisticated AI tools to create self-driving labs, in which an AI system designs and executes complex experiments, troubleshoots and tweaks protocols, and orchestrates activities across an entire lab that is chock-full of disparate equipment.
Designing such labs for molecular biology is challenging because of the field’s complex workflows, which require assorted equipment and high precision, says Haibo Chen, a computer scientist at Shanghai Jiao Tong University and a co-author of the report. “In many existing systems, human experts are still required to configure the instruments,” he says. “AI is mostly added to handle just one part of the process.”
To create a more fully autonomous lab, Chen and his colleagues decided to construct it from the start with AI in mind, rather than adding AI capabilities to a pre-existing system.
Genetic messages
The team tested AutoDNA by tasking it with a variety of projects, including detecting a cancer-linked mutation in a sample of DNA. In another experiment, the researchers asked the system to encode a message in DNA using its four nucleotide bases, abbreviated as A, C, G and T. They selected a popular quote, often misattributed to cosmologist Stephen Hawking: “Intelligence is the ability to adapt to change.”

indian-startups-1a7382a05b.headline: Razorpay receives SEBI approval for IPO
indian-startups-1a7382a05b.fulltext:
Fintech unicorn Razorpay has received approval from the Securities and Exchange Board of India (SEBI) for its initial public offering (IPO), according to sources familiar with the development.
The Bengaluru-based company had confidentially filed its draft red herring prospectus (DRHP) with SEBI in June 2026.
According to an Economic Times report, Razorpay is targeting to raise Rs 5,500-6,500 crore through its IPO at an expected valuation of $5 billion (Rs 49,000-50,000 crore).
As per sources, the company expected to file its final IPO papers before March 2027.
Media reports indicate that Razorpay has roped in Axis Capital, Kotak Mahindra Capital, JP Morgan and Citi as bankers for its proposed IPO.
Razorpay was last valued at $7.5 billion in 2021, when it raised $375 million during the peak of the funding cycle. Since then, the company has undertaken several strategic initiatives ahead of its public market debut.
In April 2025, Razorpay converted into a public limited company as part of its IPO preparations. Later that year, it completed its reverse flip to India, a process that involved shifting its domicile from the US to India. The company paid around $150 million in taxes related to the transition.
Founded in 2014 by Harshil Mathur and Shashank Kumar, Razorpay provides payment gateway services to businesses. Over the years, it has expanded into business banking, lending and payment solutions for merchants.
Most recently, Razorpay received the final Payment Service Provider (PSP) licence from the International Financial Services Centres Authority (IFSCA) to operate in GIFT City, Gujarat. The licence will allow the fintech company to offer payment services to businesses operating in the International Financial Services Centre.
Entrackr has reached out to Razorpay for comments. The story will be updated once the company responds.

A KsheerasagarPublished4 Nov 2026, 11:38 PM IST A Democratic sweep of both chambers of Congress in the midterm elections left Wall Street divided in Wednesday's trade. While AI chipmakers, memory companies and data centre operators fell, hyperscalers surged sharply. Shares of Amazon surged 8% to a three-month high, while Apple and Microsoft advanced 6% each. Alphabet gained 5.7%, while Meta Platforms climbed 3.5%, powering a rally on Wall Street after days of selling fuelled by concerns over the soaring costs of the AI boom. Apple, which has avoided Big Tech's massive AI spending but is feeling the impact of an AI-fuelled surge in memory chip prices, jumped nearly 7% to a record high. If the gains hold, the five companies are on course to add more than $750 billion in combined market value, according to Bloomberg. A Democratic-led Congress could push for tighter regulation of AI development and data centre construction. Some investors see this as a sign that hyperscalers may moderate their spending. On the other hand, SanDisk shares slumped 10%, while peer Seagate Technology Holdings plunged 8.2% at its intraday low. Nvidia, the chipmaker that quickly became the poster child of the AI stock frenzy, slipped 2.5%. CoreWeave, a company that rents out access to AI chips to customers over the cloud, fell 11%. Advanced Micro Devices, another chip giant, was down 1.5%, even after reporting a much stronger profit for the latest quarter than analysts had expected. For hyperscalers, the rally marks a sharp reversal after a difficult period for cloud giants. Their quarterly earnings reports highlighted how the race to build AI infrastructure was turning once cash-rich, debt-light companies into heavy spenders increasingly reliant on borrowing. Microsoft was a notable exception, reporting $18.6 billion in cash flow. Democrats have voiced opposition to data centre expansion, including in Texas. The results could accelerate a backlash against the power-hungry, water-intensive and noisy facilities that are central to the AI boom but have become increasingly unpopular with local communities. The tech giants have been building capacity at a blistering pace, with plans to spend more than $740 billion this year, up from roughly $400 billion last year, as per Bloomberg. The artificial intelligence industry has remained volatile for months amid criticism that valuations have risen too far and that the sector could be in a bubble. Concerns are growing that the hundreds of billions of dollars Big Tech companies are pouring into AI data centres may not generate enough productivity gains and profits to justify the investments. The latest earnings reports from Alphabet and other Big Tech companies also highlighted how AI-related investments may be weighing on their existing businesses. Google's parent company reported a larger cash outflow, as measured by free cash flow, during the latest quarter, alongside slower-than-expected growth in its search business. US President Donald Trump has been a strong supporter of the AI industry, and Democratic control of Capitol Hill could bring greater regulation or restrictions for the sector. Concerns about AI have, however, been growing across political parties. State-level policy changes could have a more immediate impact on the industry. Democrats won gubernatorial races in Ohio, Georgia and Texas, three states with significant planned data centre investments. Their incoming governors have pledged greater oversight of the sector. In Ohio, Democratic Senator-elect Sherrod Brown made opposition to data centre expansion a central part of his campaign. We want to make Codex the place where developers and agents take on their most ambitious projects.

Peppermint Robotics, which makes autonomous cleaning robots, has raised Rs 100 crore (about $10.5 million) in a pre-Series B round led by pi Ventures and Crane Venture Partners. Asiana Fund also participated in the round.
The Pune- and Austin-based startup said it doubled its revenue last year and grew nearly sixfold between FY24 and FY26. It last raised Rs 34 crore ($4 million) in a Series A round in April 2025. Peppermint has a presence in nine countries, with the US being its biggest market.

Its machines scrub floors and move materials in factories, hospitals, airports, malls, warehouses, hotels and universities. They are designed to fit into existing routines rather than disrupt workflows.
The company primarily serves facility management companies that oversee cleaning operations, including the selection of equipment, chemicals and cleaning processes.
One of its more challenging deployments is at a global pharmaceutical company, where its cleanroom robots have passed qualification testing in an EU GMP Grade cleanroom, among the most tightly regulated settings a cleaning robot can enter, Peppermint said, in a statement.
Cleanroom robots are specialised manipulators engineered to operate in controlled, contamination-free environments.

They run on proprietary Peppermint OS, using computer vision and LiDAR to map spaces, plan routes, and avoid obstacles. Operators can monitor them in real time through a cloud dashboard. The newly raised capital will go towards next-generation robotics and expanding manufacturing capacity. An assembly line in North America is also being planned over the coming months.
Peppermint also intends to step up business development in the United States and Asia, grow its presence in Europe, and hire senior leaders and engineers.
On the product side, it plans to widen its range of floor-cleaning and material-handling robots and develop its cleanroom line.
Shubham Sandeep, Partner at pi Ventures, pointed to the company's "clear ROI" in demanding settings such as healthcare and hospitality. Anandamoy Roychowdhary of Crane Venture Partners said Peppermint has built a production-grade cleanroom robot for mission-critical businesses. Written By Sayak BasuPublished4 Nov 2026, 03:21 PM IST
Google has decided to extend its employee buyout offer to several countries as it looks to cut down on other costs as the company continues to spend heavily on artificial intelligence, as per a report by Reuters.
Google, whose parent company is Alphabet, has confirmed to Reuters that it had begun offering voluntary exit packages to its employees based out of Canada, France, Germany, Japan and Switzerland.
"In 2025, some of our teams introduced a voluntary exit program with severance," a Google spokesperson said in a statement to Reuters. "This past summer, in June, we expanded this program globally in a few countries to support our important work ahead."
This move comes as Google and most of the other Big Tech companies are spending heavily on AI, which has gone on to unnerve Wall Street and bring down the stock price of Alphabet. Last week, another tech giant Microsoft, had also offered 60,000 of its employees buyout contracts to try and contain costs.
In recent quarters, the employee count of Alphabet had kept growing, but now it looks like the Sunar Pichai-run company is looking to move their resources to areas that are higher up in the priority ladder.
At the end of September 2026, Google's workforce expanded to 204,757, showing that it had added nearly 10,000 workers in a period of six months. This increased headcount, which was disclosed in the company's third-quarter earnings results, was in stark contrast to its other tech peers who were looking to bring down their number of employees as per their changing business strategies.
Notably, the acquisition of Wiz, a cybersecurity firm, in March this year, had also contributed to the increased in Google employees as they had to absorb 2,000 employees of Wiz.
This latest buyout offer comes after the exit programmes that have been offered to Google employees since last year in some divisions across the US and Britain. This programme has been described as an exit option for employees who no longer feel aligned with the path the company is taking.
As AI and cloud computing become Google's hiring priorities, employees in their Google Cloud as well as the AI unit DeepMind were kept out of the buyout offers issued in the past.
Google has around 5,000 employees in Switzerland, with a major engineering hub of the company located in Zurich.
Exit packages were offered in mid-June and employees were given till mid-July to apply for the same. Those who did, got one month's salary for every year they worked at the company, up to a maximum of 12 months.

health-tech-024d795df1.headline: The iPhone effect in healthcare: How Mounjaro is rewriting the economics of India's pharma market
health-tech-024d795df1.fulltext:
The iPhone effect in healthcare: How Mounjaro is rewriting the economics of India's pharma market
Mumbai, Nov. 4 -- For years, GlaxoSmithKline's Augmentin, a broad-spectrum antibiotic, held a place at the top of India's pharmaceutical sales charts. Its reign reflected the economics of a market built on scale, volume and affordable medicines. That pecking order has now been overturned by GLP-1 drugs, sought after for weight-loss and diabetes treatment. Eli Lilly's patented Mounjaro has emerged as the country's top-selling drug by sales.
The rise of Mounjaro points to a shift in a market long dominated by generics: Indian patients are increasingly willing to pay a premium for newer therapies-even for generics that are priced at a premium.
The entry of generic semaglutide after Novo Nordisk's patent expired in March 2026 has unleashed a surge in volumes, even though the treatment costs between Rs.1,850 and Rs.8,000 a month-hardly inexpensive by the standards of the Indian pharma market.
The trends point to a market in which affordability is still crucial, but no longer the sole determinant of choice. Brand reputation, confidence in the medicine, delivery systems and the promise of better outcomes are beginning to matter more.
For Indian drugmakers who built their businesses on making medicines affordable at scale, the implications are significant. The opportunity may lie not merely in selling more medicines at lower prices, but in building brands and treatment experiences that patients and doctors are willing to pay for. The GLP-1 drugs market could be an early indication of that transition.
The numbers underline the speed at which the category has taken off. Mounjaro, launched in India in March 2025, recorded sales of Rs.923 crore in 2025-26, according to data from Pharmarack, an e-commerce market audit company. Sales in the last 12 months to September 2026 stood at about Rs.1,736 crore. The total GLP-1 market was pegged at Rs.2,596 crore over the same period, with injectable products accounting for about 86% of the value.
GLP-1 medications are often administered via subcutaneous injection into the fatty tissue of the abdomen, thigh, or upper arm but pill-based solutions exist as well.
The entry of generic semaglutide has added another dimension to the market. Following the expiry of Novo Nordisk's patent in March, several Indian companies launched their versions of the drug. Monthly semaglutide sales rose from Rs.48 crore in February 2026 to Rs.113 crore in September. In volume terms, sales shot up nearly sixteen times, from about 114,000 units to 1,876,000 units, with generics accounting for nearly 74% of the units sold.
Vishal Manchanda, a pharma analyst from the Systematix Group, a financial services entity, estimates that the semaglutide market is now running at an annualised rate of about Rs.900 crore, while the overall GLP-1 market could be close to Rs.3,000 crore. And these are early days. "Compared to the penetration in the US, we haven't even scratched the surface yet in India," he says.
A Gallup national survey in the US put the use of GLP-1 drugs for diabetes at 11% of the adult population and that for weight loss at 15%.
The potential customer base is substantial. An ICMR-INDIAB study estimates that 254 million people in India are living with obesity and 101 million with diabetes. Not all of them are candidates for GLP-1 treatment, and the drugs are not intended to replace diet, exercise or medical supervision. But the scale of the underlying conditions gives pharmaceutical companies a large market to address as awareness, diagnosis and access improve.
The category has also benefited from a change in how obesity is discussed. Long treated largely as a lifestyle issue, it is increasingly being recognised as a chronic disease requiring sustained management. This has created room for medicines that were initially associated with diabetes treatment to become part of a wider conversation around metabolic health.
While generics lower the barrier to entry, brand perception still heavily dictates patient choices. In a category where titration takes months and individual responses vary, brand reputation often acts as a proxy for efficacy.
Aakanksha Chauhan, a 37-year-old engineer based between Mumbai and the UK, began using Ozempic in early 2025 after an endocrinologist recommended it as she prepared for an egg-freezing procedure. She says she lost 40-45 kg over six months. After stopping treatment, she regained about 10 kg. Her doctor later recommended Wegovy and subsequently Mounjaro, in the context of insulin resistance.
Chauhan also runs a GLP-1 coaching community and a WhatsApp group, where she has observed how strongly brand names can shape patients' views of the treatment. A member might report losing only 300 grams in a week on a generic medicine and ask what to do. Another user may respond by recommending Mounjaro instead, on the assumption that it is better.
"They don't realise that Mounjaro would also lead to similar weight loss.people think it is a superior drug as that is how it has been sold to the market," she says.
The exchange is not evidence that one brand is clinically superior to another. Weight loss and response to treatment vary between patients, and the choice of medicine and dose needs to be guided by a doctor. But these conversations illustrate how a brand can acquire a value beyond its active ingredient. In a market where patients are spending a significant part of their monthly income on treatment, perceptions of quality and effectiveness can carry considerable weight.
A 40-year-old Delhi resident, who didn't want to be identified, offers another perspective. He tried Sun Pharmaceutical's Noveltreat and Zydus' Semaglyn over four months, moving between doses, but did not experience the appetite suppression he had expected. Mounjaro was recommended to him, but he has been reluctant to switch because of its cost.
"It's still an ongoing process, and I haven't really figured out my ideal dose that can balance hunger suppression with side effects," he says.
He chose the brands himself, weighing reputation against price. "The endocrinologist was trying to enforce another generic brand but I went with a mix of reputed and value for money," he adds.
The experience reflects the balancing act facing patients. A lower price can make treatment accessible, but it does not necessarily remove the need to find a brand and delivery system that the patient and doctor are comfortable with. Some users prefer multi-use pens because they can lower the cost of treatment over time. Others prefer single-use pens for convenience or privacy, particularly if they do not want to store a multi-dose device at home.
There are also reports of patients seeking retatrutide, Eli Lilly's next-generation GLP-1 drug which is under phase 3 trials in the US but is reported as widely available in the grey markets.
Sambit Patnaik, a Mumbai-based consulting colorectal surgeon, says that his patients are aware of retatrutide and are sourcing it at Rs.38,000 for a month's supply. "Expectations are high from well-heeled patients who are now willing to go to any length for quick results," he quips.
One industry observer likens it to the desire to own the latest model of an iPhone. The analogy is useful, but it also captures the risk. Medicines are not consumer gadgets, and brand preference cannot substitute for clinical evidence or medical advice. Yet, the premium that patients are willing to pay for a product they perceive as better is a commercial reality that drugmakers cannot ignore.
For Indian drugmakers, GLP-1 drugs demand a departure from the traditional playbook. These are long-term injectables requiring patient familiarity with delivery devices, titration schedules, and side-effect management.
Diabetologist Rajiv Kovil cautions that companies have crowded the market with too many brands and devices. "You have 50 brands which have come out and you have almost eight to nine different kinds of devices," he says.
The proliferation has created confusion among doctors as well as patients. Kovil argues that companies should have taken more feedback from physicians experienced in injectable therapies before launching multiple devices. If doctors are not comfortable with the devices, patients are unlikely to be either. Some companies, he says, have since begun addressing the problem and rebuilding physician confidence by demonstrating the reliability of their delivery systems.
The bigger challenge is to move beyond the price competition. "In GLP-1, it's always about the durability of the prescription.retaining patients over a year is going to be the first kind of a hurdle," he says.
He believes the market could eventually resemble the statin category, where lower prices and widespread availability helped build a large base of patients.
Manchanda sees a similar shift in how companies will have to compete. "Everybody wants to get the patient directly. So there is a bit of a direct-to-consumer (D2C) shift in this category that we can see," he says.
Direct engagement, however, will not be enough. For generics, he expects word of mouth and doctors' experience with individual products to become increasingly important.
Alkem Laboratories is tailoring its approach to this dynamic. Entering the semaglutide market in March 2026 with three brands-Semasize, Obesema, and Hepaglide-the company introduced both pre-filled disposable pens and reusable devices to manage recurring costs. Sandeep Singh, managing director of Alkem, notes that improving access requires addressing ease of administration alongside affordability. To prevent dropouts, Alkem is pairing its products with support groups guiding patients on diet, exercise, and side-effect management.
The rapid uptake of GLP-1 drugs is also changing the way multinational pharmaceutical companies view India. For years, the country was often a market where new patented medicines arrived well after their global launches, in part because of concerns over affordability and commercial viability. That gap has narrowed in recent years.
"The time lines of launches of patented drugs by multinationals post the global launches has shortened from over 7-8 years to 2-3 years," says Anil Matai, director general of the Organisation of Pharmaceutical Producers of India (OPPI), which represents multinational pharmaceutical companies in India. "For MNCs, the Indian market is at an inflexion point as companies are now confident of bringing their blockbusters to India sooner. The success story of GLP-1 drugs greatly reinforces their confidence."
Lilly has sought to expand its reach through a commercial arrangement with Cipla for Yurpeak, its second brand of tirzepatide. The partnership draws on Cipla's distribution infrastructure to extend access to more patients. Lilly says its approach is not limited to bringing a medicine to market, but also includes building awareness of obesity as a chronic disease and encouraging evidence-based care.
Novo Nordisk, meanwhile, has emphasised physician confidence, affordability and dependable access. The company points to its manufacturing expertise, clinical evidence and integrated medicine-and-pen delivery system as factors underpinning confidence in its products. Its managing director in India, Vikrant Shrotriya, has said that "changing an entrenched perception takes sustained effort". The comment refers to the challenge of changing how obesity is understood, but it also captures the broader task of building trust in a relatively new category of treatment.
The interest in India is not restricted to GLP-1 drugs. Roche, for instance, has been stepping up its clinical-trial activity and broader presence in the country, with plans for more than 20 product launches or 'indication extensions' over the next three to five years across oncology, haematology, ophthalmology, neurology and infectious diseases.
Just like GLP-1 drugs were first use
